summary: Describes how deployed MPLS networks do Equal Cost Multipath and gives best practices for applications that want to avoid the packet reordering that comes from sending a flow's packets over different paths. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: If cars of one convoy take different roads, they arrive out of order. This note tells designers how to keep the convoy together.

questions: how to avoid ecmp in mpls
why do mpls routers check the first nibble
how to avoid ecmp in mpls pseudowires
subtitle: Why some MPLS payloads get split across paths, and how to define a payload so that packets stay in order.

tldr.problem: MPLS routers often guess whether a payload is IP by looking at the first nibble after the label stack. A non-IP payload that happens to start with the wrong value can have its packets spread over several equal cost paths and arrive out of order.
tldr.mechanism: Applications defining a payload over MPLS must forbid the values 0x4 and 0x6 in the first nibble. Applications that depend on in-order delivery are REQUIRED to restrict that nibble to 0x0 or 0x1.
tldr.outcome: This is a Best Current Practice (BCP 128). It is a heuristic, but it gives a relatively safe way to operate MPLS networks even if future IP version numbers are allocated.

today: RFC 4928 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2007. It has since been updated by RFC 7274 and RFC 9790, which should be read together with it.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
This document describes how deployed MPLS networks perform Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) and gives best practice recommendations for anyone defining an application to run over MPLS that wants to avoid reordering. Reordering can happen when different packets of the same flow are sent over different equal cost paths.

Disabling ECMP is an option for most operators, but few if any have chosen to, and an application designer has no control over the networks the application will run over. So ECMP is a reality that must be reckoned with.

The RFC separates two behaviors. IP ECMP picks the next hop from the header(s) of an IP packet. Label ECMP picks it from the label stack of an MPLS packet.
sections.eli5: When there are several equally good roads, routers share the cars among them. That is fine until the cars belong to one convoy that must stay in order.

sections.title: How Deployed Routers Guess the Payload
sections.content:
The MPLS label stack carries no protocol identifier. The payload is identified by the Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) of the bottom label, defined in RFC 3031. A router that only handles the labels it must process often cannot tell what the payload is.

IP networks split traffic across paths by hashing fields of the IP or contained headers, mainly or exclusively the source and destination addresses in a network core. Vendors wanted MPLS to behave the same way, so equipment guesses by inspecting the first nibble after the label stack, where an IP version number would be. If it is 0x4 (IPv4) or 0x6 (IPv6), the payload is treated as IP. Most deployed routers treat a first nibble of 0x4 as IPv4 for IP ECMP.

The consequence is that any application whose payload can begin with 0x4 or 0x6 may have its flows take multiple paths, with considerable jitter and possibly out of order. It also complicates measurement, monitoring and tracing. New payloads such as those from the PWE3 and AVT working groups are not IP and, if specified without constraint, might be mistaken for IP.

Routers that correctly see a non-IP payload usually share load using the label stack. Any reserved label can be included in the calculation, so adding an explicit null or router-alert label to a packet could change its path.
sections.eli5: A router glances at the first letter of the package. If it looks like an IP package, it feels free to send it down any road. A package that is not IP can be fooled by an unlucky first letter.

sections.title: When Being Mistaken for IP Does Not Matter
sections.content:
The RFC notes that for some applications, being mistaken for IPv4 is not harmful. The trivial case is an MPLS IPv4 VPN, where the real payload is IP and most deployed equipment will find the end of the label stack and perform IP ECMP correctly.

A less obvious case is when the packets of a flow have constant values in the fields that IP ECMP hashes. For example, if an Ethernet frame immediately follows the label and the router does ECMP on IPv4 but not IPv6, the first nibble is either 0x4 or something else. If it is not 0x4, no IP ECMP is done, although Label ECMP may be. If it is 0x4, the constant MAC addresses sit where the IPv4 source and destination addresses would be, so the hash input is constant and always gives the same result.

These cases are lucky accidents, not a design. The recommendations that follow do not depend on them.
sections.eli5: Sometimes mistaken identity does no harm, because every package in the convoy gets the same wrong label and so they all still take the same road.

sections.title: Recommendations for Avoiding ECMP Treatment
sections.content:
An Application Label is a label allocated with an FEC Type defined or used by an application. It sits at the bottom of the label stack, and its FEC Type defines the payload that follows.

To avoid being mistaken for IP, the payload format must at a minimum disallow the values 0x4 and 0x6 in its first nibble. Applications that depend on in-order delivery are REQUIRED to go further and restrict the first nibble to 0x0 or 0x1. That keeps their flows unaffected even if future equipment snoops for future IP versions.

The price is stated plainly: if an IP version with number 0x0 or 0x1 were ever defined, equipment following this BCP could not look past the MPLS headers to hash on that header. Such IP traffic would be safe from inappropriate splitting but also would not get the performance benefit.

RFC 4385 gives an example of how ECMP is avoided in pseudowires.
sections.eli5: The rule is to start your package with a mark that no road sign recognizes. Then the routers leave it alone and keep the convoy together.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The worst result of a security breach of these mechanisms would be mis-ordering of packets and the possible loss of throughput. For example, TCP connections may in some cases reduce the window size in response to mis-ordered packets. To cause even that, an attacker would need to change a router's configuration or implementation, or change the bits on the wire. Other MPLS security issues are out of scope.

IANA marked the value 0x1 in the IP protocol version number space as Reserved and added a reference to this document to both 0x0 and 0x1. The document does not change the policies for allocating version numbers.
sections.eli5: If someone tampered with this, the worst case is that packages arrive out of order. That is annoying but not dangerous.
